I quite enjoyed this game, even though poor short-term memory retention made it a bit harder than it should have been. If the idea of a terminal-based game makes you worry that it might go over your head or something similar, don't. I'm barely sapient and was able to finish the main story without much trouble.
Play it in the dark with a mechanical keyboard and six monitors for maximum effect. You are required to say "I'm in" every time you beat a level.

Despite not recommending it, it is a very decent game! Cleverly created, with lots of interesting spiraling paths and information to dig into. Though short, I got it on sale and it's more than worth the price. However, the story seems to progress in these spurts and leap that don't entirely link (what actually happened to Bit though?), and more than once you need to refer to a walkthrough to not get frustrated. Additionally, the actual gameplay is very repetitive, basically the same six commands with brief periods of waiting ( there is a counter but it's easily stopped ). If you're after the information trawling, and don't mind the frustration as you try and fail and read endlessly, then highly recommend! If you're after something that will teach you about hacking, tentative recommendation ( actual learning is better ). Overall, good game, glad I played it, not something I am going to rave about to others.

An excellent puzzle game that itself is actually fairly close to the real experience of command-line hacking. Its workshop content is excellent, offering players a number of tools to create compelling stories and challenging puzzles, even if the toolbox is a bit barer than I would like. Would buy another expansion no questions asked.

This is easily the best hacking game I've ever played. But to be fair the only other hacking games I played were Watch Dogs 1 and 2 sooooo... take that with a grain of salt. Playing this with my hood up and mask on makes me feel like a recruit for Anonymous or like I'm a character in Mr. Robot. The commands you type in to make stuff happen probably aren't realistic, since a good bit of them are one word, but its fun nonetheless. The story is interesting. I wouldn't say its the most elaborate storyline I've seen in a game, but let's be honest, nobody plays this for the plot. Currently I'm at a point where I've been fully accepted into Entropy and have just finished my first contract. It took me a while to figure some of the puzzles out, but once you get past them you feel mentally powerful. The soundtrack is on point, if I do say so myself. I like synthwave music, and the dev made a great soundtrack for the game. They fit the mood perfectly, and they alternate on missions. There hasn't been a song on here that I didn't like. They're chill, but ominous. Perfect! I got this on sale for $1.99, but $10 seems like a really good price for this. Great game, would reccomend

The game design works at first, and there are timed missions when you really get into the action – musics do their job. You have kind of a sense of accomplishment as you get your hands on more "hacking" tools and get to face bigger challenges. There is quite a lot of humorous content on the side – not in the main story! – and that's appreciated because it's not far from being a text game.

But that's about all the nice things I can think about this game. Pretty soon, you reach its limits and the sense of accomplishment fades away. If you have no feeling for IT stuff, you may get lost pretty fast. But if you're too much into it, the game mechanisms are very disappointing. The main idea was good, but the execution rather bad. If you're still curious, I'd suggest to buy it on sale.

The difficulty relies on: 1. The cryptic aspect of computers – you'd better know the basics about file system and console ;  2. Timed challenges ; 3. Finding little bits of information (user name, password, IP...) here and there among text in files and mail ; 4. Systematically scan the targets in all ways possible. That's not something that keeps one entertained for long.

The console, which you use a lot, is rather rudimentary. At the very least it should have felt like a real one and at least to go smoothly when you type. The cursor is glitchy, not always showing where it actually is. Key pushes may be repeated when hold a few microseconds too long. The number of commands is very limited. They are sometimes buggy when not used as intended. Managing the in-game files is pretty tedious, there are no commands for creating/deleting directories. There is no way to make scripts or shortcuts. At best you can rename the executables. By the way, having "exe" files on a Linux simulation is an heresy.

The graphic interface lacks functionalities too. It would be great if you could move and resize the panels, especially the one for the "netmap" which gets pretty packed and hard to read after a while. You may find an in-game executable which helps a little bit with that. Also content will overflow from panels when too big. Why no copy/paste available?!? It would have been so useful. I grew tired of retype every user name, password and IP. Plus there are some links that are meant to be open in a real browser (as eater eggs only).

The game mechanisms are very limited. Some special missions or events break the monotony, but the player are not prepared for them either. [spoiler]For instance you are not likely to be able to defend your computer against other hackers.[/spoiler] The hacking tools are also limited in number, in versions and they almost all work in the same way. Missions are quite alike, and you're doing the same dull things over, and over, and over...

They tried to make up for it with the game story, but it turns out to be a bit déjà vu, corny, and even a bit predictable.

Two alternatives would have been preferable for making such a game:
— Either make it more approachable, even less realistic but with a more pleasant game design. Then it would need hacking to be more like puzzles.
— Or make a game for nerds, where the in-game computers can be configured, where files matter, with better console commands and executables, even maybe some scripts to edit.

The entire game keeps you on your toes and fully interested in the questline, from the tutorial, to porthacking porthack.heart and Bit's final message, and then throws in so many little nuggets of fun that give you a reason to look around on everybody's computer. The last quests throw so many challenges based that to solve you must use all the techniques you learned. It took me a good thirty minutes to figure out that I needed to use eosDeviceScan on Prometheus, and another thirty minutes to remember that all eOS devices had the password "alpine." It's a good hacking simulation game, but I couldn't bring myself to like it. The game is short, probably will take around 6 hours to finish. The mission objectives were very unclear, I had to use a guide to finish the game. The NetMap was really horrible, everything was cluttered, and it was so hard to use. I couldn't understand the story much. The contract missions felt repetitive for me. Sometimes hacking a PC doesn't save the credentials and I had to hack the same PC multiple times even when looking at my mailbox. About 90% of time, you'll be writing 'Shell, Porthack, Analyze, SSHcrack, FTPbounce' etc. And on top of that you're given just a measly 800 MB ram PC... are you kidding me???

Looking on the bright side, there're definitely plenty of surprises in the game. I mean for real. I used a guide, so it was ruined for me. You'll definitely get stuck at some point of the game. The visual effects were really good. The music went well with the game.

It's a fantastic game. The developers did an amazing job at giving the player an actual feel of what's it like to be a very skilled and powerful hacker. Soundtrack is great and fits in very well.
